name: Katharine Bradley
bio: Poet, born 1846, the elder half of "Michael Field" and the aunt of her collaborator and life partner Edith Cooper (1862-1913), whom she raised. "Michael Field" is not a person but the single joint pen name under which Bradley and Cooper published everything: eight volumes of poetry, some twenty-seven verse dramas, and a joint diary, Works and Days. Wilde addressed his letters to "Michael Field", writing to the pair as one correspondent. Bradley and Cooper came from a well-off Birmingham family, read classics at University College, Bristol, and lived together first in Reigate and finally in Richmond; on the Y90s account Bradley was the older and the more glamorous and expansive of the two, and was "Michael" (also the Simiorg, or All-Wise-Fowl) in the private mythology of the diary. Wilde corresponded with "Michael Field" between 1890 and 1893 about their verse dramas and about placing A Question of Memory with J. T. Grein's Independent Theatre. Bradley survived Cooper by less than a year and died in 1914.
bio_note: Dates (1846-1914) from the editors' identifying footnote to Wilde's letter to "Michael Field", Complete Letters (2000), p. 449, read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03 (the editors print the forename "Katherine"; the roster form "Katharine" follows the Y90s biography and her own usage).

sources.quote: Dear Michael Field, Write to Miss Elisabeth Marbury, c/o Low's Exchange, New York City, USA. She manages all my plays. I have written to her. I am a wretch not to have answered sooner, but I have no excuse; so you will forgive me. Your third act was quite admirable - a really fine piece of work - with that touch of terror our stage lacks so much. I think the theatre should belong to the Furies. Caliban and Silenus, one educated and the other sober, seem now to dominate, in their fallen condition, our wretched English drama. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to 'Michael Field', [? late October 1893], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. He is helping them place a play in America and praising their third act. The Caliban and Silenus line is Wilde on the contemporary English stage.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde acting for them professionally, and what he thought of their play.
